about: The C# counterparts of the Java API references of the guide Solving Graph Problems with Graphity (https://github.com/kaufco/graphity-doc), which links every name of the Java API to the API documentation of the language a reader picks. One entry per public or protected type, constructor and method of the four published Java modules, keyed by its declaration as java-refs.txt lists them: 'name' is the name in C#, 'url' its page and anchor relative to the root of the API documentation (docRoot when built here, https://kaufco.github.io/graphity-csharp/ when published), and 'note' what a reader of the Java text would not expect. Where C# keeps Java's overloads of a method as several overloads of one name, 'signature' is the name with the parameter list of the overload, without the return type, as the API documentation shows it, so that the guide can tell them apart; Java's overloads that are one method in C# keep the plain name and share its url. Where C# has no counterpart, 'name' and 'url' are null and 'reason' says why. ApiMappingTests in tests/Graphity.Examples.Tests checks the entries, and every url and signature against the API documentation when it is built.
docCommand: dotnet tool restore && dotnet docfx docs/docfx.json --warningsAsErrors

SortedIntView.listIterator(int).reason: .NET has no list iterator, which moves both ways from a position. A SortedIntView is indexed with view[i], and enumerated from a position with foreach over view[index..].

SortedIntView.spliterator().reason: .NET has no spliterators and no streams to split for. A SortedIntView converts to ReadOnlySpan<int>, which Slice cuts into parts without a copy, and is an IEnumerable<int> for LINQ and PLINQ.
